item.title: Syria’s Leader, Though Strengthened, Faces Tests as He Addresses U.N.
item.description:
When President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria addressed the United Nations General Assembly last year, he was still in the throes of transforming his image from a rebel leader who once had ties to Al Qaeda into a head of state ushering in a new era in a country ruled for decades by dictatorship.

He returns to New York this year in a much stronger diplomatic position, and is scheduled to be the first speaker before the Assembly on Wednesday morning. Mr. al-Sharaa has secured significant sanctions relief, extended his government’s authority across most of Syria and gained international acceptance among a broad spectrum of foreign leaders, including President Trump.

Now, Mr. al-Sharaa now faces a more difficult test: turning those diplomatic ties into tangible gains for Syrians as mounting economic and security challenges threaten to undermine the country’s transition.

Syria’s economy remains in crisis and the flood of foreign investment his government hoped would quickly follow sanctions relief has not yet materialized. The World Food Program estimates that the monthly cost of essential needs for a family of five — including food, utilities and basic services — rose by almost 33 percent between June 2025 and June 2026.

The rising cost of living has deepened public frustration with Mr. al-Sharaa’s government. Last week, government increases in fuel prices triggered the country’s most widespread protests since Mr. al-Sharaa took power nearly two years ago, forcing his government to partially reverse the increases.

Mr. al-Sharaa is also struggling to restore Syria’s sovereignty in the face of Israel’s increasingly entrenched military presence in the south. Earlier this month, a U.N. commission investigating Syria reported that Israeli military operations in southern Syria had deepened, with repeated incursions, patrols, raids and searches disrupting civilian life. It warned that some Israeli actions, including the detention of Syrian civilians, could amount to war crimes.

Israel’s presence in southern Syria reflects its broader shift in defense strategy toward establishing military buffer zones beyond along its borders, including in southern Lebanon and Gaza. But its military activity in Syria is also bound up in a growing rivalry with Turkey, one of Mr. al-Sharaa’s closest allies and a longtime supporter of the rebel movement he once led.

Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the war in Gaza began in 2023. Turkey’s deepening military ties with Damascus have heightened Israeli concerns about the prospect of Turkish forces and equipment operating in Syria. Israel has struck Syrian military facilities that Turkey had assessed for possible use, underscoring the potential for Syria to become a flashpoint between the two regional powers.

Mr. al-Sharaa’s government has broken with its predecessors to express an openness to engage with Israel and has taken part in U.S.-mediated talks with Israeli officials in the hopes of easing tension. But that diplomacy has not yielded a security agreement or an Israeli withdrawal from southern Syria. And at a U.N. Security Council meeting last week, Syria’s permanent representative to the U.N., Ibrahim Olabi, also accused Israel of responding to Syria’s efforts at diplomatic engagement with “airstrikes, incursions and violations.”

“Israel penetrated our villages, displaced our people, bombed our facilities while we chose to spare the region further suffering,” Mr. Olabi said.

item.title: The Secret History of Bats: A New Study Redraws Their Family Tree
item.description:
Bats are cryptic creatures. They inhabit the dark, roosting in hidden, often inaccessible places. And they possess some rare skills that can seem like superpowers: exceptional longevity, advanced echolocation abilities and a capacity for powered flight that is unique among mammals.

But their genes have been difficult to decipher and their fossils hard to find, leaving scientists puzzled about how these traits evolved — or even when and where bats first emerged.

A major new study — the largest analysis of bat genomes and fossils — sheds light on the origins of these mysterious mammals. The study, which was published on Wednesday in the journal Nature, suggests that the first bats emerged in Europe roughly 65 million years ago and that echolocation emerged early, before bats diversified into the many families existing today. It also presents a new evolutionary tree for bats, one that upends some previous conclusions about the relationships between different bat families.

The findings are “rewriting” the biological history of bats, said Ariadna Morales, an evolutionary biologist and research associate at the American Museum of Natural History and an author of the paper. “The evolutionary tree of bats changed.”

The study — which is the first phase of the Bat1K project, an effort to sequence and analyze the genomes of all living bat species — also lays the foundation for additional research into the underpinnings of their remarkable abilities.

“Bats are the most extraordinary of all our mammalian lineages,” said Emma Teeling, a zoologist at University College Dublin and a director of the Bat1K project, who is an author of the new paper. “This is a springboard.”

Bats are numerous, diverse and widely dispersed. There are roughly 1,500 living species of bats, which account for more than one-fifth of all mammal species, and they live on every continent but Antarctica.

For the study, scientists collected and sequenced the genomes of bats from 103 different species, spread across all 21 living families of bats. Then, they analyzed these genomes, and compared them with one another, using a variety of approaches. Some involved analyzing the full genomes of each species; others compared specific chromosomes, regions or other subsets of the data.

“Different parts of the genome tell different stories,” said Dr. Morales, an incoming assistant professor at the City University of New York.

But several lines of evidence converged, allowing the researchers to map the evolutionary relationships between different families of bats.

The resulting phylogenetic tree differed from previous ones in some notable ways. The sucker-footed bats of Madagascar, for instance, had been grouped with several bat families that live mostly in the neotropics. The new tree moved these Madagascar bats to the globally distributed superfamily that also contains vesper bats, the most common bats on the planet. The findings also suggested that this vesper bat superfamily was closely related to the superfamily containing sac-winged bats, whose members had previously been considered more distant relatives.

The researchers also analyzed bat fossils, using the data to estimate when different lineages had diverged and how bats spread across the globe.

Europe, Africa, North America and Asia had all been proposed as the birthplace of bats, but the new analysis pointed toward Europe. From there, bats most likely expanded into Africa and then to the rest of the globe, the researchers concluded.

The study also suggested that the fossil of an extinct echolocating bat belonged close to the base of the evolutionary tree — and that echolocation appeared before the modern lineage of bats did.

Scientists have long debated whether echolocation or flight evolved first in bats. One influential study, based on a 52-million-year-old fossil and published in 2008, suggested that flight evolved first.

But the new analysis, which is based on a much larger data set, indicates that the question is far from settled.

“It looks pretty clear that echolocation evolved before the diversification of all the living families,” said Nancy Simmons, a curator emerita at the American Museum of Natural History who is an author of the new paper, as well as the 2008 one.

“Now we’re sort of back where we were a number of years ago, which is flight and echolocation seem to have evolved at the base of the tree,” she added. “And we still don’t know whether they came at the same time, or one came before the other.”

The researchers said that they hoped that their new evolutionary tree would be a resource for scientists studying the genes and genetic variants that underpin flight, echolocation, disease resistance and more. That work is already underway at Bat1K, Dr. Teeling said.

“To be able to uncover evolutionary history is extraordinary,” she said. “But there’s so much more we can do with this.”

item.title: Walkouts Are a Longstanding Tradition at the U.N. General Assembly
item.description:
Nearly 200 world leaders get a lectern and two microphones to make their point at the United Nations General Assembly. The 1,000 or so lower-ranking diplomats in the hall have to settle for more limited options for self-expression: Stay seated or leave.

Walking out has become something of a tradition in recent years. On Wednesday, the lone U.S. diplomat in the hall left his seat as President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran accused the United States of targeting his country’s civilians. It was a mirror image of the day before, when the Iranian delegations’ seats were nearly empty as President Trump described the choice he said he faced with Iran: make a peace deal or “annihilate” the country.

The Cuban delegation also exercised its right to leave the hall on Wednesday. As Mr. Trump labeled the country a “failed state” and vowed to bring about the downfall of its government, four Cubans stood up and walked briskly to the exit.

Rosa Freedman, a professor of law at the University of Reading in England who specializes in the United Nations, said walkouts were a permitted form of diplomatic protest that U.N. delegates had practiced for decades. “So long as it’s done peacefully, then there are no rules that prevent states from walking in and out,” she said.

For over 70 years, walk out they have. During the throes of Algeria’s war for independence from France throughout the 1950s, French diplomats left the hall when the body raised the conflict — something Paris held was none of the U.N.’s concern. In 1956, Hungary’s delegation walked out of the General Assembly after the Soviet invasion of Budapest. When South Africa’s foreign minister defended his country’s system of racial apartheid in a speech during the 1964 session, diplomats from about 40 countries staged a walkout.

When President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad of Iran repeated incendiary conspiracy theories in 2010, suggesting that the United States had orchestrated the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, delegates from over 30 countries walked out, including the American diplomats.

Last year, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel delivered his address before a sea of empty chairs, as many diplomats refused to take their seats in protest of Israel’s war in Gaza. Once Mr. Netanyahu started speaking, the number of diplomats who walked out was so high that they had to form a line to reach the exit.

Conducted peacefully, Professor Freedman said, walkouts are an important expression of freedom of speech and assembly, hallmarks of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted soon after the body’s founding. She also noted that in comparison to parliamentary chambers, the General Assembly can be hectic.

“People are constantly walking in and out of the rooms and walking around the rooms, sometimes on mobile phones,” she said. “The filing out from the room in protest does not have the same level disruption as it would do in a parliamentary body, where everyone keeps their seat for the duration of a session.”

item.title: Zelensky Is Expected to Warn Russia’s Aggression Won’t Stop at Ukraine’s Borders
item.description:
When President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine addressed the United Nations General Assembly for the first time after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, his appeal for international support was fueled by raw moral indignation.

Mass graves in the newly liberated Ukrainian city of Izium had just been uncovered, and the atrocities in Bucha and other reclaimed towns continued to shock the international community. “A crime has been committed against Ukraine, and we demand just punishment,” he declared in a prerecorded video address.

When Mr. Zelensky takes the stage on Wednesday, he will no longer be pleading merely to awaken the world to the war’s horrors, but also demanding the means for his nation to survive and warning that the violence will not remain confined to Ukraine.

On Tuesday, he met with President Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York and said that he hoped Russia’s war in his country would end “before winter” and that the Trump administration would help Kyiv do it.

“I think we need to do this as quick as possible — before winter,” Mr. Zelensky said. Mr. Trump nodded and repeated his words with approval.

Mr. Zelensky’s speech will most likely revisit core themes from his previous addresses, including global food security, the urgent need for advanced air defenses, and warnings about the proliferation of artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems in warfare.

“We are now living through the most destructive arms race in human history,” he told the General Assembly last year.

The early consequences of that race are already clear. Escalating destructive capabilities on both sides can been seen in brutal frontline combat that kills or wounds thousands of soldiers every month and in relentless long-range bombardment campaigns.

Mr. Zelensky is also expected to reinforce his consistent message that Russia’s aggression will not stop at Ukraine’s borders.

Moscow is already testing how far it can push abroad, analysts say, strangling global grain routes to pressure the developing world while waging a brazen campaign of arson, sabotage, and cyberattacks across Europe.

Mr. Zelensky has frequently argued that Russia and its key partners — North Korea and Iran — seek to dismantle the American-led security architecture established after World War II and are the primary agents of chaos in a world beset by crises.

His diplomacy faces added complexity, however, given Mr. Trump’s disdain for the traditional alliances that served as the backbone of global stability.

Mr. Zelensky must navigate a delicate political line: invoking what were once the foundational values of American foreign policy without alienating an administration pursuing an approach starkly different from its predecessors.

As America has pulled back from its traditional role, European democracies have struggled to fill the void.

Mr. Zelensky is expected to argue once more that securing the continent requires defeating Russian forces in Ukraine and degrading Moscow’s capacity to wage war.

Four years after the invasion, civilian casualties from Russian strikes have surged. through a relentless daily toll: a family killed when a missile hit its home at midnight; two people killed in a drone strike at a gas station; five dead after a public bus is struck.

As Ukraine prepares for what may be the most challenging winter of the war, Mr. Zelensky must convey the critical urgency of his nation’s plight to world leaders increasingly distracted by competing global crises and domestic political pressures.

item.title: Stanislas Hutin, Who Denounced Torture in France’s Algerian War, Dies at 95
item.description:
Stanislas Hutin, whose firsthand account of witnessing torture by French troops in the Algerian war of independence helped incite a wave of revulsion against that losing conflict, died on Sept. 2 in Arradon, in Brittany, France. He was 95.

His death was announced by Ouest-France, a large-circulation daily newspaper that Mr. Hutin’s father founded after World War II.

Mr. Hutin’s testimony — published anonymously in June 1956 and soon republished by well-known French antiwar writers — was among the earliest to chronicle the systematic torture practiced by French forces against Algerians attempting to free themselves from colonial rule, and it was among the most influential.

Mr. Hutin was a 24-year-old Jesuit seminarian when he was conscripted in 1955. His army unit, the 21st Colonial Infantry regiment, was sent as part of a “pacification” effort — he used the phrase derisively in a 2019 interview — deep into the Algerian countryside.

He was a most reluctant recruit, as he made clear in the interview, conducted by the historian Tramor Quemeneur for the national audiovisual archive. Mr. Hutin, a machine-gunner, said, “I wrote a text before I left” France, “pleading with the Lord that this machine wouldn’t spit death because of me.”

After disembarking from his troop transport, he was shocked by the poverty of the Algerians and the brutality that his officers displayed toward them. Beatings of suspects were the order of the day, but much worse was to come.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

He was preparing to go to sleep in his tent, in a French encampment in Algeria’s northeast, on a cold night in late January 1956, when he was startled out of his bed.

“The cries of a pig being slaughtered I heard last night around 9 p.m. came, indeed, from the young boy,” he began his journal entry for the next day. The boy was a shepherd of 14 whom the French soldiers had captured two days earlier.

“At first I thought it was the jackals,” he wrote in the little red spiral-bound notebook he kept, clandestinely. “But it kept going on and on.”

“So I got out of the tent in my pajamas and listened: voices and groans were coming from the lieutenants’ tent. I said to myself: ‘They can’t possibly be subjecting that kid to the magneto.’ ” (That was the name of the troops’ portable field generator, which had often been put to sinister use: Wires from it were attached to various parts of a victim’s body, notably the testicles. And it left no detectable trace of torture.)

“I went back inside, once more broken and sickened,” he wrote.

“It was the boy,” he continued. “This morning, I’m literally shattered.”

Already considered a “Communist” by the officers in his unit, “I really got into it” with the lieutenant who had done the torturing, he told Mr. Quemeneur years later. “A brute, a sadist,” he wrote in his journal the next day.

He took a picture of the teenager, Said Boutout, “to show to people in France” the face of the French army’s brutality: a curly-haired boy so youthful he barely looked 14.

The photo of the teenage Said, who survived the ordeal, later appeared on book covers. “It became, for me, a real memorial of this abominable war,” Mr. Hutin told Mr. Quemeneur.

Mr. Hutin was back in France by the spring of 1956, and that June, a Jesuit priest published excerpts from Mr. Hutin’s journal in the order’s publication L’Action Populaire.

The following year, as opposition to the Algerian war was growing, extended portions appeared in a short collection of testimonials, “Des Rappelés Témoignent” (“Recruits Testify”), published by a group of Christian intellectuals.

Also in 1957, Pierre-Henri Simon, a Catholic writer who became Le Monde’s literary critic, published “Contre la Torture” (“Against Torture,” not translated), including extracts from Mr. Hutin’s journal. It was a book that “marked an entire generation,” the Catholic journalist Jean-Claude Petit wrote when it was republished in 1999. And the eminent classical historian and antiwar activist Pierre Vidal-Naquet cited him extensively in his book “La Torture dans la République” (1972).

For Mr. Hutin, the small red notebook and the letters he had written to his family, served a private, not just public, purpose. “My family, journalists, when I came back, they wanted to know,” he told Mr. Quemeneur. “It allowed me to liberate myself from this traumatism. It was a real catharsis.”

Stanislas Hutin was born in Rennes, France, on Sept. 7, 1930, the third of five sons of Paul Hutin-Desgrées, a journalist, World War I veteran and leading figure in the Mouvement Républicain Populaire, the Christian-democratic party that became a force in post-World War II politics. His mother was Magdeleine Desgrées du Loû.

Journalism ran in the family: Mr. Hutin’s maternal grandfather had founded the newspaper L’Ouest-Éclair at the end of the 19th century, the ancestor of Ouest-France.

Mr. Hutin’s father was imprisoned by the Germans in 1943. “We were continually confronted by the occupying forces,” Mr. Hutin recalled in the 2019 interview. Friends in the Resistance were shot by the Germans, a memory that shaped his reaction in Algeria later.

In 1951, he entered the Jesuit order and three years later was drafted to serve in Madagascar, another African colony that France was vainly trying to hold on to. On his return, he helped compose a report exposing slavery on a Madagascar coffee plantation. The report gained some attention because his father was by then a member of the French Parliament.

Sent to Algeria in the summer of 1955, he was designated for service as a teacher by the French army, as part of the “pacification” campaign. He recalled in the 2019 interview that “the captain ordered me to keep a rifle next to the blackboard, a flagrant contradiction.”

He left the Jesuits after the war — it ended in 1962 with France’s humiliating defeat — studied sociology and ethnology, and pursued a career aiding commercial development and banking in developing countries, especially Africa.

He is survived by a brother, Gonzague Hutin.

In the late 1970s through ’80s, when he returned to Algeria as a development worker, Mr. Hutin sought out Mr. Boutout, the teenager who had been captured and abused. They ended up establishing a rapport, Mr. Quemeneur said.

In his retirement, he spoke frequently in French schools about the lessons of the Algerian misadventure. “He was someone of great humanism,” Mr. Quemeneur said of Mr. Hutin. “He was open to others, and open to dialogue. He accepted the positions of others. And he dedicated his life to the service of others.”

item.title: Iran Will Not Be Bullied, President Says in Defiant U.N. Speech
item.description:
Iran’s president delivered a defiant speech at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday, vowing his country would defend itself until “its last breath” and would not give up its civilian nuclear program. At the same time, he left the door open for negotiations with the United States.

Directly addressing President Trump, who on Tuesday called Iran a leading sponsor of terrorism and threatened to annihilate it unless a deal was struck, President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country would not succumb to bullying.

“Iran must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue, diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force,” Mr. Pezeshkian said at the end of his speech.

Iran is the first country to have a head of government attend the General Assembly in New York while that nation is at war with the United States, the host of the U.N. headquarters. Mr. Pezeshkian used the diplomatic stage to present Iran’s point of view.

“We need power, because a people who doesn’t have power will be crushed in this war,” he said. “We will not ask permission from anyone for defending our country.”

Mr. Pezeshkian held up photographs of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed by an Israeli strike on the first day of the war; elementary schoolchildren killed in Minab by American airstrikes; and athletes and children killed in a U.S. strike on a sports stadium.

“Iran must be powerful to avoid being threatened, to avoid its future being threatened,” he said. “Our defensive systems have been built so that no one can think that bombing Iranian cities will go unanswered.”

The United States and Israel launched a surprise attack on Iran in February amid negotiations between Tehran and Washington over Tehran’s nuclear program. A big sticking point in the talks had been whether Iran would get to keep a civilian nuclear program, enriching uranium at a very low level. Mr. Trump had said he wants zero enrichment and facilities closed.

The war has created new flash points, including the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway that Iran effectively closed, resulting in a spike in oil and energy prices and disruptions in global supply chains.

Mr. Pezeshkian reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to a peaceful nuclear program. “For our country, peaceful nuclear technology is part of our inherent progress,” he said.

Mr. Pezeshkian slammed Israel, saying the country had nuclear weapons, conducts cross-border attacks on other countries, including his own, yet faced no punishment.

“Then they call us the terrorists?” he said, adding, “Israel kills and Iran is sanctioned.”

Mr. Pezeshkian contended that Iranians had been demonstrating “every night” over the past seven months in support of their country. While hard-line supporters of the Islamic Republic have held nightly rallies since the start of the war, the same crowds have attacked the president and negotiating team and have opposed a deal with the United States.

A large number of Iranians who oppose the government also took to the streets in a nationwide uprising in January and were gunned down, with security forces killing at least 4,200 protesters, rights groups say.

Despite the heated rhetoric by Mr. Trump and Mr. Pezeshkian, their representatives worked on the sidelines of the U.N. session to find a way forward.

On Tuesday, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, held an hourslong meeting, mediated by Qatar, with Mr. Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and they discussed resuming negotiations and a way to de-escalate.

Ismael Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry, who is also in New York, said Iran had also talked about its conditions for reviving diplomacy, which includes ending the U.S. naval blockade on Iran, releasing the country’s frozen assets and ending hostilities on all fronts.

These conditions were the backbone of a 14-point peace agreement that Iran and the United States signed in June, but it quickly fell apart after Iranian hard-liners, in an attempt to upend the deal, launched attacks on ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz.

Mr. Trump has since said that the Memorandum of Understanding he signed with Iran is invalid and he wants a more comprehensive deal.

item.title: At Trump’s Request, Nations Are Designating Crime Groups as Terrorists
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that President Trump had asked leaders of a new coalition of 18 nations across Latin America and the Caribbean to label two dozen crime groups and cartels in the region as terrorist organizations.

Such moves could help provide a public rationale for the U.S. military to conduct strikes on the groups, either on its own or in partnership with the security forces of those countries.

Mr. Trump made his request at a group meeting in New York on Tuesday with leaders and top officials from the countries. The meeting took place on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly.

“Obviously, some countries are in the process of doing it,” Mr. Rubio said of the terrorist designations. “Some have already done it. They all have different laws internally as to how they can reach that designation point, but the Shield of the Americas is about defeating these transnational criminal groups.”

The Shield of the Americas is the name of the coalition, which has a total of 19 nations, including the United States, formed to fight drug traffickers. Peru, which Mr. Rubio visited this month, is the latest country to join.

Many of the nations are run by right-wing or conservative governments that have voiced public support for Mr. Trump’s military attacks in Latin America and the Caribbean, including airstrikes on civilian boats that are widely deemed to be extrajudicial killings by legal experts.

Mr. Rubio’s comments, made to reporters in a news conference in New York, confirmed a New York Times article on Tuesday that 14 nations in the coalition had agreed to make a terrorist designation on crime groups at the urging of the Trump administration. Each nation has its own process for doing that, and leaders might need to seek approval from legislative bodies.

The two dozen crime groups have already been designated foreign terrorist organizations by the State Department. That designation gives the U.S. government the power to restrict financial transactions by the groups or their associates, but it does not provide a legal basis for military action.

After The Times published its article on Tuesday, the State Department announced that 14 countries in the coalition and the United States were taking joint action on crime groups, including “sanctions, designations and financial actions.”

The announcement included a list of two dozen crime groups, but two organizations in Colombia were grouped together into one listing.

item.title: Zelensky Warns Russia’s War Will Expand if It Is Not Ended Soon
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine called on Wednesday at the U.N. General Assembly for more sanctions and other measures to halt Russia’s “ridiculous and never-ending war” before it entered another deadly winter. If the fighting isn’t ended, he warned, Russian aggression would soon spread to other parts of Europe.

“Russia’s finances and Russia’s production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped,” Mr. Zelensky said, referring to the Russian leader, Vladimir V. Putin, and arguing that Poland, Moldova and other neighboring countries would be next. Artificial intelligence could soon make the war more deadly and unpredictable, he said, adding, “We need peace before we reach that point.”

Mr. Zelensky said that Ukraine had no choice but to escalate its attacks against Russia, whose military has increasingly targeted energy and civilian infrastructure. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelensky. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia, too.”

Mr. Zelensky had met with President Trump earlier on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the General Assembly, and had said then that Ukraine hoped for a cease-fire “before winter.”

Still, Russia’s foreign minister, speaking at a Security Council meeting on Ukraine before Mr. Zelensky’s speech, made clear that the likelihood of a cease-fire were slim.

The minister, Sergey V. Lavrov, rejected the possibility of an interim peace agreement or a pause in fighting, while blaming Europe for the full-scale Russian invasion of its neighbor in 2022 that set it off.

“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” said Mr. Lavrov, using Russia’s preferred euphemism for the war. He said a cease-fire would only allow Ukraine to shore up its defenses. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and just wants to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons,” he said.

Mr. Lavrov’s statements appeared to dash hopes for diplomacy between Russia and Ukraine, even as the United States has been working on getting the two sides to the negotiating table.

Earlier this month, President Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, traveled to Moscow to meet with President Putin and then made their first trip to Ukraine to speak with officials there.

The war in Iran, which the United States started with Israel in late February, has dragged on much longer than Mr. Trump had initially pledged it would and has pushed the fighting between Russia and Ukraine lower on his administration’s list of diplomatic priorities.

Mr. Trump has called for Russia and Ukraine to halt strikes on energy sites, and his administration appears intent again on persuading both sides to restart negotiations.

At the Security Council meeting, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, reiterated a call for a cease-fire but noted that there was a limit to the usefulness of statements and meetings. “So many speeches have been made in this council, so many right words, but the war drags on,” he said.

Mr. Sybiha said the war was a concern beyond Ukraine’s borders. “We must stop this war now before Putin enters your home,” he said. “He is already at the entrance.”

Other officials at the Security Council meeting castigated Russia. France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, accused Russia of “lashing out at Europe in its entirety,” and of violating international law by attacking Ukrainian civilians and civilian infrastructure and by flying drones into the airspace of European nations.

Ed Miliband, the British foreign minister, called for Russia to engage in diplomacy, arguing that it was failing in the war. “Even if morality does not sway the Russian government, reality should,” he said.

Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said that “the world is losing” as long as the conflict continued, and sought to persuade the Council that Russia and Ukraine had areas of “common ground” that could lead to “reasonable, incremental” steps toward peace. He did not directly address Mr. Lavrov’s statement rejecting any sort of pause in the fighting.

Mr. Zelensky had said ahead of his visit to New York that he planned to discuss “de-escalation proposals” with Mr. Trump. Before he addressed the General Assembly on Wednesday afternoon, he posted on social media about a series of Russian attacks on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, and in other parts of the country overnight.

“At every meeting during the U.N. General Assembly, we are working to ensure continued support for Ukraine,” he wrote. “Equally important is the fair pressure exerted on Russia through sanctions.”

Reporting was contributed by Farnaz Fassihi, Max Bearak and Pranav Baskar.

item.title: Decoding Trump-Xi
item.description:
If it feels like Donald Trump and Xi Jinping just had a meeting, you’re not wrong. It’s their third in less than a year. But every time the leaders of two superpowers get together, it’s a big deal, and today’s meeting at the White House is a state visit. Lots of pageantry. Will there be substance? We’ll see.

Today’s newsletter is a guide to the Trump-Xi meeting.

Who is going into this visit with the upper hand?

Probably Xi.

Trump is facing a midterm election in which his party is far behind in polls and he is stuck in a war that voters don’t like. Xi, as our China correspondent David Pierson explains, is gearing up for a “norm-shattering fourth term as head of the ruling Communist Party.” He’s going to be in power for at least another five years.

Trump and Xi face very different political realities. Trump really doesn’t want a trade fight before an election. The Chinese economy may be struggling — but Xi doesn’t answer to an electorate.

What should we expect to come out of the state visit?

For all the pageantry that typically surrounds Trump-Xi meetings, they don’t produce much.

David again: “Xi appears to have calculated that the best way to manage the United States is to engage Trump in high-profile summits rich in optics but thin in substance.”

Expectations are low for breakthroughs on anything significant like A.I. safety or Chinese trade imbalances. But maybe China will agree to buy more U.S. agricultural products, like it did last time. (Xi promised in May to buy more U.S. farm goods, but that hasn’t happened.)

There’s currently a trade war truce. Is it holding?

More or less. But that doesn’t mean that relations have been without conflict.

Scott Bessent, the U.S. Treasury secretary, has described the relationship as “a water polo match” in which leaders are basically following the rules. But under the surface, he said, China was doing “a lot of kicking,” and “if we have to, we’ll kick back.” An editorial in a Chinese state-run newspaper called that a “perfect metaphor,” but it said it was the United States that was doing the kicking.

Among the flash points, according to my colleague Ana Swanson, who covers trade: China is unhappy about U.S. bans on importing Chinese cars and humanoid robots. The U.S. is unhappy about those unfulfilled farm goods promises. China wants more access to the powerful chips required for cutting-edge A.I. models — part of the two countries’ ongoing race to control the future of that technology. And, of course, China’s control of rare earths is still looming over the relationship.

How did China get to the point where it could compete with the U.S. on A.I. in the first place?

Through lots and lots of government spending. My colleague Vivian Wang has a big story on this, well worth reading in full. Basically, 10 years ago, Xi began a push to turn China into the world’s dominant producer of A.I., a place where artificial intelligence permeates daily life. “To realize that vision,” Vivian writes, “the Chinese government is mobilizing the full weight of the state.”

In contrast to the A.I. industry in the U.S., which has been funded by hundreds of billions of dollars in private investment, “economists estimate that Chinese state-led funds put more than $184 billion into A.I. firms between 2000 and 2023, and last year, the government and state-owned banks pledged hundreds of billions more.”

That has put China in a competitive position in the A.I. race. (Take a look at where the U.S. has the upper hand on A.I. and where it’s lagging behind China.) The spending might, however, be having consequences for the broader Chinese economy, which is looking weaker than it has in decades, as my colleague Li Yuan writes. As the government pours money into A.I., it isn’t doing enough to boost employment or consumption, economists say.

Watch David Sanger, our White House and national security correspondent, explain in the video below how the U.S. and China can contain their A.I. race.

And how does Taiwan fit into all this?

As one analyst recently told my colleagues: “There’s only one issue that could cause relations between both sides to break down completely or erupt in conflict, and that is Taiwan.” China has long claimed the self-governed island as its territory, and Taiwan relies heavily on U.S. military power to ward off the threat from Beijing.

Analysts expect Xi to try to persuade Trump to keep delaying $14 billion in proposed U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, a deal that Trump has described as “a very good negotiating chip.”

What might this chip be used to bargain for? Trump might want China to increase pressure on Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Taiwan just surpassed China as the third-largest source of U.S. imports, behind Mexico and Canada, according to U.S. figures. The bulk of those imports are — as you might have guessed — semiconductors and other technologies related to A.I.

In a defiant speech, Iran’s president vowed that his country would defend itself until “its last breath,” but he left the door open for negotiations with the U.S.

President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia’s “ridiculous and never-ending war” in Ukraine would soon spread to other parts of Europe.

The U.N. has “kindly reminded” world leaders to limit their addresses to 15 minutes. If history is any indication, that guidance will be ignored.

Tigrayan forces in Ethiopia seized a key airport in the city of Mekelle, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.

Two centrist parties were the front-runners in Morocco’s legislative elections, which had been overshadowed by migration and the frustrations of young people.

Outside the “Worried West,” most people around the world are curious or excited about A.I., according to a new poll.

Dolly Parton’s manager accused her nephew of threats, extortion and intimidation in the wake of her death.

Stanislas Hutin, who chronicled the torture used by French troops in the Algerian war of independence, died at 95.

item.title: Trump’s Board of Peace Lays Out 6-Month Plan for Gaza That Faces Roadblocks
item.description:
President Trump’s Board of Peace put out a new short-term plan on Wednesday to begin rebuilding the Gaza Strip, even as prior efforts have led to little progress on the ground.

At a briefing in New York, the board — created in January as a central player in Mr. Trump’s plans for the territory — laid out a six-month, $2.45 billion blueprint to decommission weapons in Gaza, clean up debris, provide humanitarian aid and establish a transitional government.

But officials acknowledged that reconstruction funds from international donors have yet to be disbursed. And Israel rejected an earlier plan announced by Mr. Trump and released by the board in July. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the proposal, which called for Israel to halt its military operations in Gaza except to defend itself against immediate threats, would jeopardize Israel’s national security. Hamas had agreed to its part of the deal, under which it would gradually dismantle underground weapons depots and relinquish its arms to an interim governmental body under the Board of Peace.

Parliamentary elections in Israel next month, when Israeli voters will decide whether to extend the rule of Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative coalition, have complicated the board’s work, according to Nickolay Mladenov, a member of the board’s Gaza Executive Committee. “Our discussions with Israel right now are not easy, because of the elections there,” he said on Wednesday. “Everything is a bit more emotional, a little bit more politically sensitive.”

The Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately return a request for comment on the elections and negotiations with the Board of Peace. Jonathan Harounoff, a former spokesman for Israel at the United Nations, blamed the lack of progress toward a deal on “Hamas’s refusal to demilitarize.”

Israel reduced much of Gaza to rubble in the wake of lethal Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and has continued launching attacks and restricting humanitarian aid in Gaza despite a cease-fire announced in October of last year. Since then, strikes that Israel portrays as operations against Hamas operatives have killed nearly 1,400 people in the enclave, according to the latest U.N. report, citing the Gaza Ministry of Health, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

The plan announced on Wednesday would spend more than $1.2 billion on infrastructure redevelopment, including humanitarian shelters and debris clearance, and nearly $900 million for “peace and security” in the first six months after a deal is reached. Board officials stressed the importance of bolstering Gaza’s infrastructure and increasing aid ahead of the winter. And Aryeh Lightstone, a senior adviser on the board, said a fund would be announced “in the very near future” for donors to contribute money toward education, culture and sports in Gaza.

Mr. Trump has framed the Board of Peace as a more effective alternative to the United Nations, but it is facing many of the same challenges that have long hampered the U.N.’s peacemaking efforts in the Middle East. The U.N. Security Council paved the way for the board’s existence in November. Wednesday’s briefing occurred not far from U.N. headquarters during the General Assembly.

The board, which Mr. Trump may chair in perpetuity according to its charter, includes heads of state — including Mr. Netanyahu — and is led by top Trump administration officials, including Marco Rubio, the secretary of state; Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law; and Steve Witkoff, the president’s special envoy to the Middle East.

But the real impact of the board so far appears to be limited. “The board seems to facilitate a little bit of communication between Israelis and other people engaged in trying to bring aid to Gaza,” said Max Rodenbeck, a researcher at the International Crisis Group in Brussels. “But they don’t seem to facilitate any actual, clear improvement in the conditions in Gaza.”

Mr. Kushner responded to reporters’ questions about the criticisms of the board’s apparent inaction on Wednesday, saying that preparations were needed to negotiate agreements and plan an effective transition of power in Gaza.

“We’re just refining, sharpening the ax,” he said, “getting ready for when we get the time to cut the tree.”

item.title: After Warm Meeting With Trump, Venezuela’s Leader Is Set to Address U.N.
item.description:
When Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, takes the stage on Wednesday evening to address the United Nations General Assembly, it will be the first time a Venezuelan head of state has done so in person in eight years.

And her speech, which is expected to highlight her interest in international cooperation, is likely to sound radically different from one delivered by her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, in 2018, when he railed against U.S. sanctions and abuse of power.

It is likely to contrast even more sharply with the most famous speech a Venezuelan leader has delivered at the U.N. — a 2006 appearance in which President Hugo Chávez called President George W. Bush “the devil” who thought he ruled the world.

Ms. Rodríguez’s presence this week at the U.N. in New York in many ways crystallizes the dizzying about-face her government has undergone in the last nine months.

For a generation, her government positioned itself as the political foe of the United States, the socialist counterweight to what it called a capitalist imperialist nation. Then the United States captured Mr. Maduro in January, and Ms. Rodríguez began to build a very public alliance with Washington. Since, Venezuela has become a de facto vassal state, with its finances and much of its resources managed by the Trump administration.

Her one-time ally, Mr. Maduro, now sits in a jail in Brooklyn, awaiting trial on federal charges of narcoterrorism, while Ms. Rodríguez is being greeted with smiles and handshakes in Manhattan. (It is unlikely Ms. Rodríguez will visit him.)

On Tuesday, she met with President Trump, posing with the U.S. leader as he flashed a thumbs up. She called the meeting “historic” in a social media post and said that the two had discussed “strengthening the bilateral relationship” and advancing cooperation on energy, mining and security.

“We expressed our gratitude to President Trump,” she continued, for “steadfast support” following major earthquakes in June.

During the meeting, Mr. Trump called for a new election to take place in Venezuela, according to a U.S. official speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the meeting, which the person described as positive and brief.

Ms. Rodríguez responded to Mr. Trump by agreeing to a vote, according to the official.

Representatives from the Venezuelan government did not respond to requests for comment. The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

For years, Mr. Maduro had not attended the U.N. event, the globe’s most important international forum, over concerns that he could be arrested while visiting New York. Instead, he addressed global leaders via video or sent emissaries.

Now, Ms. Rodríguez will take the stage in a speech closely watched by diplomats and business executives around the world. Just last month her government agreed to an oil deal that gave the United States enormous control over 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s oil, about a fifth of its resources.

Before she became interim president, Ms. Rodríguez played a central role in the government of Mr. Maduro. For years watchdogs have accused that government of egregious human rights abuses.

Just days before Mr. Rodríguez arrived in New York, a U.N. mission charged with investigating those abuses published a report that said that “state institutions responsible for repression, gross human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain fundamentally intact” under Ms. Rodríguez.

Venezuelans in the United States and Venezuela have protested her visit to the United Nations, calling on the Trump administration to pressure Ms. Rodríguez to hold a new presidential election.

While Ms. Rodríguez is being greeted in Washington, Venezuela’s most popular opposition leader, María Corina Machado, says that she continues to be blocked from entering her country. Ms. Machado left Venezuela last year to attend the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony.

Apparently trying to highlight the contrast between her freedom of movement and that of her country’s authoritarian leader, Ms. Machado’s allies said she made three failed attempts to enter Venezuela on Tuesday.

“During the last 24 hours, María Corina Machado has been denied entry into Venezuela three times,” said David Smolansky, a representative. “She has attempted to enter the country by air and sea but has been turned away each time.”

Mr. Smolansky did not specify who had blocked Ms. Machado’s entry.

In New York this week, Ms. Rodríguez has tried to cultivate the image of a soft, personable leader concerned about the state of the world, said Phil Gunson, a Venezuela analyst for International Crisis Group.

Ms. Rodríguez arrived, he noted, wearing a jacket featuring the image of Mafalda, a plucky cartoon character famous in Latin America for being “distressed about all the cynicism and the violence and the censorship,” he said.

The real Mafalda — if she existed — would probably be distressed to see her image used by Ms. Rodríguez, he added.

In her speech, Mr. Gunson predicted that Ms. Rodríguez might make “some nods in the direction of a kind of leftism — but they’re going to be very muffled.”

“Geopolitically, obviously Delcy is now completely bound by the pact with Trump,” he continued. “She’s essentially trying to conciliate the boss.”

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Xi’s Visit Will Fuel More Scrutiny Over His Health
item.description:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, arrives at Joint Base Andrews, every step he takes down the stairs from his plane will be scrutinized for clues about his health.

Mr. Xi is China’s most dominant leader in decades: He is preparing to claim an all-but-certain fourth term in power from late next year, and there is no sign of a likely successor waiting in the wings. And at 73, Mr. Xi is old enough that any stumble or missed meeting ignites speculation abroad about his health. (The topic is heavily censored in China.)

No matter what happens on the stairs or during Mr. Xi’s three-day visit to Washington, guesswork about his health and probable longevity is sure to persist.

China’s Communist Party does not have clear rules of succession if a leader becomes incapacitated or dies, and Mr. Xi magnified the uncertainties by overturning retirement norms. Mr. Xi’s predecessor, Hu Jintao, retired in 2012 at 69, and his cognitive decline appeared visible in 2022, when he was abruptly escorted from his chair at a party congress, looking confused and upset.

In August, Mr. Xi stepped slowly down the stairway of his plane, holding his wife’s hand, when they visited Kyrgyzstan, igniting rumors online about his health.

The discussion intensified this month after he skipped a dinner at a regional leaders’ meeting in New Delhi. Mr. Xi was absent from a dinner for the BRICS group of developing countries — which includes Brazil, Russia, India and China — according to Indian news reports and a diplomat from one of the participating countries.

There was no suggestion that Mr. Xi was seriously ill. When he left New Delhi, he climbed the stairs to his plane unaided. Still, the absence fed questions in some foreign news reports about Mr. Xi’s health and stamina.

Mr. Xi is a bulky man who has said he became a smoker from his youth in the Chinese countryside, but details of his lifestyle are unclear. A friend of Mr. Xi told U.S. diplomats in 2009 that Mr. Xi, then preparing to succeed Mr. Hu, “did not drink or do drugs,” according to a diplomatic cable disclosed by WikiLeaks.

But Dennis Wilder, a former C.I.A. senior analyst who tracked Chinese leaders, told The Wall Street Journal that Mr. Xi had a reputation as a frequent drinker and longtime smoker who did not like to exercise.

Mr. Xi has not publicly commented on his health or plans for retiring or staying in office. Last year, he was inadvertently caught on a microphone chatting with Russia’s president, Vladimir V. Putin, about living forever. “People rarely lived to be over 70, but these days, at 70, you are still a child,” a man who appeared to be translating Mr. Xi’s remarks to Mr. Putin was recorded saying in Russian.

Whatever his health, Mr. Xi gets some of the most attentive medical care in the world. Chinese leaders have their own health care system that provides round-the-clock care and checkups at elite hospitals, including the military-run 301 Hospital near the leadership’s headquarters in Beijing.

item.title: Canada’s Capital Bids Good Riddance to Trump Avenue as Tensions With U.S. Rise
item.description:
Call it the lake effect.

Take away a body of water steeped in Canadian pride, as President Trump attempted when he ordered the federal government last month to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and reprisals from the north seemed bound to follow. Even from reputedly mild-mannered Canadians.

A backlash on a smaller scale came on Wednesday when the City Council in Ottawa, Canada’s capital, voted unanimously to remove Trump Avenue as the name of a residential street, the latest in a cross-border geographic spat that is making mapmakers’ heads spin.

The street is one of several in Ottawa’s Central Park neighborhood that were named for New York City institutions when it was developed in the late 1990s and early 2000s, long before Mr. Trump started a trade war with one of America’s closest allies.

And long before Mr. Trump audaciously suggested making Canada the “51st state” and imposed crippling tariffs on it.

“I don’t like the idea of anything that’s named for Donald Trump, who has demonstrated hostility towards Canada,” Mark Sutcliffe, Ottawa’s mayor and a council member, said at news conference after the vote.

The motion passed unanimously to change the name of the S-shaped street, which has about 65 homes on it and intersects with some other roads whose names might be familiar to New Yorkers, including Whitestone Drive and Bloomingdale Street.

John Germano, 65, a retiree who has lived on Trump Avenue since 2010, said in a phone interview on Wednesday that his address had become a dubious distinction, especially when ordering deliveries.

“It’s embarrassing, like they just chuckle and laugh,” Mr. Germano said.

He added, “It gets worse and worse every day.”

A working group of several Trump Avenue residents will help create a list of potential replacement names, said Riley Brockington, a City Council member who is spearheading the change.

Mr. Brockington said the erasure of Mr. Trump’s name from the street was not intended as retaliation for Mr. Trump’s bid to rename Lake Ontario but in response to what he described as the president’s attacks on Canadian sovereignty and the carnage caused by his economic policies.

“He does not deserve the honor of having his name on a city of Ottawa street,” Mr. Brockington said. “We’re the nation’s capital.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Pete Hoekstra, the United States ambassador to Canada, who has been the subject of a petition effort seeking to expel him that has been signed by more than 200,000 Canadians, declined to comment on Wednesday.

Canada has at least eight other places with the name Trump in them, though those are not named after the president. Still, some have sought to change those names, too.

Two of them, East Trump Lake and West Trump Lake, can be found in Cochrane in eastern Ontario, according to the Canadian Geographical Names Database, which registered their origins in 1973.

Peter Politis, the mayor of Cochrane, said in an email on Wednesday that the lakes are in an unorganized township under provincial control. Not that renaming them hasn’t crossed his mind.

“That said, as mayor, I am sorely tempted to wave the mayoral pen and table a motion anyway, given how fitting it feels at the moment,” he wrote.

Mr. Politis mused that he might not stop there.

“On a tongue-in-cheek note, we’ve toyed with the idea of renaming our local landfill dump ‘Trump,’” he wrote.

Sudbury in Ontario is home to Trump Lake and Trump Creek, names that the Canadian Geographical Names Database recorded as originating in 1954.

Shortly after Mr. Trump’s executive action to rename Lake Ontario, Michel Lalonde, 36, a D.J. from the city of Sudbury, started a petition to rename Trump Lake. He said on Wednesday that he had never visited the lake, which is roughly six hours northwest of the city.

“The whole thing has become absurd and ridiculous,” he said.

Mr. Lalonde lamented the deterioration of U.S.-Canada relations.

“I just so wish we would go back to how things were 20 years ago,” he said. “It’s just an unfortunate stain on a relationship and an unfortunate stain on our history.”

In Ottawa, Mr. Brockington of the City Council said he had previously surveyed residents of Trump Avenue about changing the street’s name during the Covid-19 pandemic but they were divided. The opponents were concerned about the administrative hurdles associated with changing addresses, he said.

But after Mr. Trump returned to the White House and antagonized Canada, he said, momentum built for the change.

“This is not a tit for tat for Lake Ontario,” Mr. Brockington said. “At some point,” he added, “you have to take a stand.”

Mr. Germano said he was hoping to play a role in the selection of a new street name.

“We love New York,” he said. “We love Americans. It’s just that one person.”

He said he had kicked around some new names for Trump Avenue: Times Square, Strawberry Fields, Upper West Side.

“I’d go for Hell’s Kitchen,” he said.

item.title: America’s A.I. Leaders Warn U.N. of Possible Peril Absent a Global Response
item.description:
Executives from America’s leading A.I. companies warned on Wednesday that the technology they helped create could pose severe challenges to society, telling world powers that international cooperation was needed to control its future development.

The U.N. Security Council, the diplomatic body tasked with safeguarding stability and peace, convened its first meeting on artificial intelligence amid rising global concerns that the technology is spiraling out of control.

But the Council has been divided over which global A.I. measures, if any, should be enforced, with the United States and China showing little interest in slowing down development amid deep mutual suspicion.

The meeting, during the General Assembly, featured remarks from OpenAI’s Sam Altman and the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei.

Speaking separately, the A.I. executives said that the fears about the technology were not misplaced, and pleaded for urgent attention from the world’s governments to ensure that it progressed safely and remained under human control into the future.

Their dire assessments stood in stark contrast to President Trump’s remarks to the U.N. a day earlier, in which he condemned a “globalist scheme” to strangle and control A.I. and vowed to not rein in the technology.

Mr. Altman, appearing in person and speaking for about 10 minutes, said the conversation around A.I. had shifted markedly in recent weeks as rapid progress in the technology’s development had made its “upside more tangible, but also the stakes and risks more immediate.”

Speaking in a measured tone as he read from prepared notes, Mr. Altman said the world had a choice. It could harness the power and promise of A.I. to usher in a “new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray,” he said.

Acknowledging the recent frenzied debates about whether A.I. could threaten human existence, Mr. Altman said: “It doesn’t matter whether people put the risk of catastrophe at 10 percent or 1 percent or 12 percent or 0.1 percent. None of these levels are remotely acceptable.”

Mr. Amodei, speaking after Mr. Altman, warned in more vivid terms that A.I. could soon pose a threat to the human race and called for a global slowdown of the technology’s pace of advancement, echoing some of his own recent statements on A.I. safety.

Mr. Amodei’s push for restraints on A.I. was embraced by Mr. Altman as well as the SpaceXAI chief Elon Musk and other senior figures in the A.I. industry.

“I believe that this is the most important global security issue facing the world today,” said Mr. Amodei, who appeared remotely via video. “If managed poorly, I even believe that A.I. could be a risk to humanity as a whole.”

He urged the Security Council to begin by supporting “narrow agreements,” including a ban on using A.I. to make biological weapons, and standards for evaluating and verifying A.I. capabilities. Finally, he called for common global standards for testing A.I. models for their risks of loss of control, and a notification system for misuses that are “significant to global security.”

Mr. Altman and Mr. Amodei, whose rival companies are both heading toward initial public offerings that are expected to tally into the trillions of dollars, stressed the need for global collaboration with the A.I. industry to ensure that the technology remains safe and that its powers are not concentrated in too few hands.

While they have each vowed to commit their companies to a range of safeguards, including voluntary reviews of powerful new models by the U.S. government before their public release, both said their industry needed support from democratic countries to build stronger rules going forward.

“No leader, no company and no nation can manage this alone,“ Mr. Amodei said. Mr. Altman, striking a similar chord, said that “if A.I. is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone.”

The U.N. conversation took place just hours before the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, was scheduled to arrive in Washington for a state visit with Mr. Trump. The two men, leaders of the world’s A.I. powerhouses, were expected to discuss the technology’s advancement, alongside a host of other issues.

Despite a fevered interest in recent weeks in the potential for A.I. to pose catastrophic risks to humanity, expectations for a major breakthrough between the two countries on A.I. remain low.

Neither Mr. Altman nor Mr. Amodei mentioned China or specifically discussed the U.S. race against the country during their addresses. Both countries are permanent members of the Security Council and have veto power.

Artificial intelligence jumped to the top of the agenda this year at the United Nations General Assembly. Secretary General António Guterres held a conference on global governance for A.I. on Monday and urged countries leading the technology to cooperate on developing safeguards “that protect us all.”

The U.N. has said it considers A.I. technology and the need for oversight as urgent as other global issues that it has taken leadership in tackling such as climate change.

But the United States told the Council on Wednesday that while it supported dialogue and diplomacy on A.I., it rejected attempts to regulate it.

Michael Kratsios, who leads the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said the Council could not oversee a technology that it did not understand and that dialogue could not be allowed “to drift toward global governance.”

“As President Trump said before the General Assembly yesterday, the United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a global scheme of control of super intelligence,” Mr. Kratsios said, using the new term for A.I. that Mr. Trump adopted this week.

China told the Council that the international community should work tougher to steer A.I. in positive directions but forcefully rejected any attempts to regulate it, saying countries had the right to develop technology based on their needs.

Russia questioned whether A.I. was relevant to the Security Council’s mandate, suggesting that it should be discussed in forums with expertise on the topic.

France and Britain, two of the five permanent members of the Council, both called for global oversight.

“We cannot abdicate our responsibility to our citizens, because we cannot outsource to private companies the first duty of government to protect our people, whatever the issue,” said Edward Miliband, the British foreign minister.

item.title: Mark Carney’s Balancing Act
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said that he had prepared over the past year for the “extreme tail risk” that President Trump might order military action against Canada, but disclosed that the two men have spoken “frequently,” even since trade talks collapsed last month, describing a tense, evolving relationship.

In a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times at its headquarters in Midtown Manhattan on Wednesday, Mr. Carney described in meticulous detail how he was systematically reducing Canada’s reliance on the United States for key technology — from space satellites to fighter jets — in an effort to make his country far less vulnerable to American threats. He outlined a plan to diversify Canada’s relationships and suppliers, and said that even with a different future president “we will be a better partner for the U.S. because of what we are doing.”

He talked about reducing reliance on Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite systems; considering alternatives to buying F-35 fighter jets; and a focus on deepening economic — though not defense — relationships with China. Mr. Trump’s exploitation of Canadian dependency on American products had taught the country a bitter lesson: “There’s certain things, once you’ve seen them, you can’t unsee them.”

When pressed on whether he took Mr. Trump’s threats to make Canada a 51st state seriously, Mr. Carney suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of a U.S.-led military invasion, but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” said Mr. Carney, a former central banker for Britain and Canada who approaches the world by meticulously assessing worst-case scenarios and drafting responses. He added: “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare.

Mr. Carney spoke for an hour on a variety of challenges, including artificial intelligence, trade, and Canada’s role as a “middle power.”

Over the past year, he has emerged as the most prominent global leader to take on Mr. Trump. Along the way, he has also begun to define a path toward reducing dependence on a superpower neighbor that he has come to regard as predatory. Around the world, other leaders have looked to him as a model for dealing with an erratic, unreliable ally — one that remains, in Canada’s case, critical to national defense and economic survival.

But few of those leaders have articulated their interests as clearly as Mr. Carney, who used a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year to describe a strategy for dealing with the rupture. “Either you retreat wholly into yourself or you diversify,” he said then, making the choice he faces stark.

Still, Mr. Carney said he speaks “frequently” to Mr. Trump and that they had spoken “a number of times” since trade talks broke down last month.

“From my perspective, we have a good relationship in the sense of we can pick up the phone and talk to each other about issues,” he said on Wednesday. “He’s direct. I’m direct in terms of where positions are. It’s much more efficient that way, and so you know that exists and that will continue to exist.”

The Canadian leader made the case, too, that in many ways, what’s good for Canada is also good for the United States because of their decades-long integration that has created stability and prosperity. Mr. Carney gave the example of the automobile industry, which is highly integrated across the U.S.-Canada border but has been at the center of the Trump administration’s tariff policy against Canada.

“My entire life, and I’m 61, we’ve had an integrated auto sector,” Mr. Carney said, adding that breaking that deep connection to repatriate all auto production to the United States is not good policy. “We think it doesn’t make sense,” he said.

Mr. Carney said that a path remains to resuming negotiations with the United States that would revive the trade agreement that fell apart in late August. Since then, the two countries have imposed rounds of tariffs on each other, and rhetoric has been menacing, particularly from Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly called Canada’s leadership “nasty.” But Mr. Carney brushed that off.

“Is there a mutually beneficial trade deal between Canada and the U.S.? Absolutely, absolutely there is one,” Mr. Carney said. He said that he was interested, for example, in adding potash to the talks. Canada provides almost 90 percent of all potash, the key ingredient for fertilizer, imported into the United States. Earlier this week, Mr. Trump said that he wanted to replace Canada’s supply with potash from Belarus — an authoritarian state aligned with Russia that is under U.S. sanctions for its role in the war in Ukraine.

Mr. Carney said that Canada, the United States and potentially also Mexico could become “fertilizer independent” by securing special access to Canada’s potash, the world’s largest reserve. He added that the Canadian option was clearly better than buying potash elsewhere that would then need to be transported through the Black Sea or the Strait of Hormuz.

“I think this is a doable component of the deal, and there are other examples that exist, and we’re ready to work toward,” he added.

At home, Mr. Carney has come under pressure to use Canada’s most sensitive and important export to the United States — energy — as leverage in the trade war. Some 60 percent of all oil imports into the United States come from Canada, while the country is also a major source of electricity for American households and industry.

Mr. Carney said he was very reluctant to limit, tariff or otherwise curb those exports to the United States.

“If you’re a reliable partner and you supply energy or food to somebody it keeps running, it’s a very, very, very high threshold to change that,” he said. “Never say never, but it starts from a position of, we need to be a reliable supplier in all cases.”

Although optimistic that efforts to strike a trade deal could be revived, Mr. Carney said he was cleareyed about areas where Canada needs to reduce its dependence on the United States.

“Starlink, we will diversify away from, no question,” Mr. Carney said, referring to the American-based cluster of communication satellites, run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, that have revolutionized the industry. He alluded to past disruptions and to Mr. Musk’s reluctance to provide Ukraine with data that would enable it to target parts of Crimea and Russia.

He acknowledged that other satellite network options are still less capable and resilient, but added that “from a defense perspective, and certainly pooled with other partners, Europeans, Koreans potentially, you get to scale and you cut that dependency.”

The Canadian government is reviewing a planned order of 88 Lockheed Martin F-35 jets and is also considering a counterproposal to acquire Swedish Saab Gripen fighters. Mr. Carney did not specify where he was on that decision, but he did say that he wanted to use Canada’s newly bolstered defense budget to order aircraft that perform well in the Arctic.

“It is a real decision because of differing capabilities, because of strategic dependencies, and because of the economic return,” he said.

Mr. Carney on Wednesday also reiterated his long-held view that a global financial system wholly dependent on the U.S. dollar was unsustainable. A move to a multipolar system in which there are several reserve currencies would “provide more flexibility,” he said.

He acknowledged that there was a “directional shift” underway in which countries were re-evaluating their exposure to the U.S. dollar, but he conceded that any pivot would be limited until there was “proper liberalization” of China’s currency and financial system. Still, Mr. Carney said he expected the demand for U.S. dollar alternatives to grow, in part because of the Trump administration’s decision to rewire trading relations and use integration as “leverage.”

“It’s the ‘fool me once, fool me twice’ point,” Mr. Carney said. “Once you see that, then you start to think, how do I diversify away?”

item.title: Carney Says Risk of an A.I. Catastrophe Is ‘Above Zero’
item.description:
President Trump has defiantly dismissed risks associated with artificial intelligence, calling the warnings that the technology could cause grievous harm a “hoax.”

But Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada staked out a decidedly different view Wednesday, saying that the probability of doom, the metric some A.I. researchers use to assess catastrophic risk, was “above zero.”

Debate over the risks of A.I. have roiled governments and leading tech in recent weeks, splitting executives, officials and workers between those who want to slow down to better control the technology and those who want to speed up to unlock new capabilities.

Mr. Carney, who has clashed with Mr. Trump on trade and other issues, was at odds with the president again on A.I., siding with those urging caution first. In a wide-ranging interview with The New York Times on Wednesday, he laid out his vision for how the global community should regulate A.I. development.

Mr. Carney drew parallels to the financial system, arguing that guardrails could stave off undue risk-taking, which could otherwise prove costly if left unchecked. He pointed to a recent incident in which A.I. agents developed by OpenAI went rogue and hacked into Hugging Face, an online library of A.I. models.

“This was all predictable,” Mr. Carney said.

He added: “It’s not a perfect analogy, but you cannot have an unregulated financial sector without having a crisis, right? It’s just the nature of finance that people push it and push it and push it and push it, and so you end up in a crisis.”

Mr. Carney backed the creation of an international body that functioned like the Financial Stability Board, an organization of central bankers and other officials that he chaired between 2011 and 2018.

The Financial Stability Board, created in 2009 in the wake of the global financial crisis, has helped to establish global standards for banking regulation.

“You have some sense of shared responsibility,” Mr. Carney said. “Personally, I think that is the right model.”

Mr. Carney’s call for an international body to coordinate on A.I. stands in contrast to Mr. Trump’s evaluation of the industry. Last week he rejected calls from leading tech executives for new limits on the technology, saying the industry already has the only guardrail it needs: “a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.”

Mr. Trump reiterated that position Wednesday during his speech at the United Nations.

“The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” he said.

He said that regulation would only serve to bolster China’s efforts to advance its own A.I. technologies — while also calling on the world to follow his lead and change the name from artificial intelligence to “super intelligence.”

“Whoever wins super intelligence, wins,” he said. “That’s the group that wins. And we’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way.”

But Mr. Carney, who has worked to mend Canada’s relations with China since taking office, took issue with the suggestion that the Chinese had no incentives to join efforts at regulating A.I. He suggested that the Group of 20, the collection of the world’s largest economies, could foster international collaboration on A.I. risks.

“I would note the U.K. is going to be the G20 president next year and has the world’s leading A.I. safety unit,” Mr. Carney added.
